title: Eggs that broke
teaches: Peregrines, DDT and poisons that build up the food chain

blocks.text: In 1960 British pigeon racers complained that peregrine falcons were killing too many of their birds, and asked for the falcons to be controlled. The government's Nature Conservancy asked a young botanist and bird-watcher, Derek Ratcliffe, to find out how many peregrines there were. He and a network of volunteers spent 1961 and 1962 visiting the cliffs where peregrines had nested before the war. Instead of too many falcons, they found too few. Fewer than half of the old nesting sites were in use, and in the south of England the birds had all but gone.

At the nests that remained, Ratcliffe kept finding something strange: broken eggs, and parent birds eating them. Peregrines had not been known to do this. He wondered whether the shells had become too weak to bear the weight of a sitting bird. Egg collecting had been a popular hobby for a century[^collectors], and museums and private collectors held thousands of peregrine eggs with the date and place each was taken. So Ratcliffe went through the collections and weighed the shells.

blocks.caption: A peregrine falcon, the fastest animal alive in its hunting dive.

blocks.text: A shell's thickness can't be measured without breaking it, so Ratcliffe used its weight divided by its length times its breadth, an index that tracks thickness. From 1900 until 1946 the index barely moved. Then, in eggs laid in 1947 and after, it dropped by nearly a fifth, and it stayed down. Sparrowhawks' eggs showed the same sudden fall. He published the result in 1967.

Something had changed in the countryside in 1946 and 1947, and it had to be something that reached a falcon that eats only other birds. The likeliest was DDT, the insecticide that had been used in the war against lice and mosquitoes and then sold to farmers and gardeners from 1946. A few years later the falcons were hit again. From 1956 British farmers dressed their seed with aldrin and dieldrin, newer insecticides that killed seed-eating pigeons outright, and the peregrines that ate the pigeons died as well. The shells gave the clue to one poison and the dead adults to the other.

blocks.caption: The peregrine and the pesticides, in Britain and North America. Press Play, or drag through the years.

blocks.text: Very little DDT was sprayed on any one field, and almost none of it reached rivers and lakes. Yet the birds at the top of the food chain were carrying a great deal. In 1966 the American ecologist George Woodwell and colleagues measured DDT and its breakdown products in a salt marsh on Long Island, near New York, which had been sprayed for mosquitoes for twenty years, and published the results in 1967. The water held 0.00005 parts per million. The plankton held about a thousand times that. Small fish held more again, the fish that ate them more still, and an osprey's egg carried 13.8 parts per million, more than a quarter of a million times the water.

The reason is lesson 10's pyramid. An animal burns most of what it eats and builds only about a tenth of it into its own body. Most chemicals leave with the waste. But DDT dissolves in fat, not water, and the body can hardly break it down or get rid of it, so it stays in the fat. A fish that eats ten kilos of smaller fish to grow one kilo of its own keeps most of the DDT in those ten kilos. Each step up the chain multiplies the poison again. This is called **biomagnification**.

blocks.caption: A poison in a salt marsh, step by step up the food chain, on a scale where each mark is a hundred times the last. Black dots are what Woodwell's team reported in 1967. The bars are a model: at each step after the plankton, food eaten times the share of poison kept.
blocks.task: Guess, then find a poison that doesn't build up

blocks.text: In the birds' bodies DDT breaks down into a closely related chemical, DDE, which lasts just as long and interferes with the gland that lays down the calcium of the eggshell[^dde]. A bird of prey can carry enough to survive, and still lay eggs so thin that they crack under it, so few chicks hatch. The worst-hit birds were those at the top of long chains: peregrines, ospreys, bald eagles, brown pelicans and sparrowhawks.

In 1962, while Ratcliffe was counting empty nests, the American biologist and writer Rachel Carson published *Silent Spring*. She gathered the evidence that pesticides sprayed to kill insects were killing birds, fish and other animals, and building up in food chains, and she warned of a spring with no birdsong. The chemical industry attacked her, but the book sold widely and led to hearings in the United States Congress[^carson].

Over the next twenty years the persistent pesticides were restricted and then banned for most uses: dieldrin and aldrin in stages in Britain from the 1960s, DDT in the United States in 1972 and in Britain in 1984. In 2001 an international treaty, the Stockholm Convention, restricted them worldwide, though DDT is still allowed for spraying the inside of houses against malaria mosquitoes. The levels in birds' eggs fell, slowly, since the chemicals took years to leave the soil and the food chain.

The peregrines came back. In Britain they were breeding again on almost all their old cliffs by the 1990s, and then on cathedrals and power stations. In North America, where the eastern birds had died out altogether, Tom Cade at Cornell University bred peregrines in captivity and released them from 1974, some of them from city buildings, whose tall ledges suit a cliff-nesting bird with pigeons to eat. In 1999 the peregrine was taken off the United States endangered list.

In Seattle a pair nested on a downtown office tower in 1994, the first known in the city, and peregrines have nested on Seattle's buildings and bridges since. They are among the clearest successes of the pesticide bans. Other persistent chemicals have taken DDT's place in the story. The killer whales that live in Puget Sound eat salmon at the top of a long food chain, and they carry some of the highest levels of PCBs, industrial chemicals that build up the same way, of any animals measured[^orca].

blocks.title: Outside
points: In spring, look up at the tall buildings and bridges of a city near you, or along sea cliffs. Peregrines nest on ledges and scrapes. Listen for a harsh repeated cry, and watch for a stocky falcon diving at pigeons. Local bird groups often run nest cameras you can watch online.

blocks.caption: Five questions on poisons in food chains
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: How did Ratcliffe show that peregrine eggshells had become thinner?
choices: He weighed eggs kept in old collections, each dated
He broke fresh eggs from wild nests
items.why: Collectors had kept dated eggs for a century. Weight over length times breadth tracks thickness without breaking them.

items.ask: Why does DDT build up from step to step in a food chain?
choices: It stays in fat while most of the food is burned
Predators prefer to eat poisoned prey
Each animal makes more DDT from its food
items.why: An animal builds about a tenth of its food into its body but keeps most of the poison from all of it.

items.ask: In Woodwell's marsh, roughly how many times more DDT did the osprey's egg carry than the water?
choices: About a quarter of a million times
items.why: 13.8 ppm against 0.00005 ppm. A thousand times is the jump from water to plankton alone; each step up multiplied it again.

items.ask: Which kind of poison would not build up the food chain?
choices: One the body breaks down or sheds quickly
One sprayed only in small amounts
items.why: If little of the poison stays in the body, each step passes on less, not more. Small amounts of a lasting poison still build up.

items.ask: Why were adult peregrines dying in Britain from the late 1950s?
choices: They ate pigeons poisoned by seed dressings like dieldrin
items.why: Thin shells cost them chicks. Dieldrin and aldrin on seed killed the adults themselves.

summary: **Britain's peregrines crashed after the war.** Ratcliffe's 1961 to 1962 census found fewer than half the old nest sites in use.
**Their eggshells thinned in 1947.** Weighing dated eggs in old collections showed a sudden fall of nearly a fifth.
**DDT and its product DDE thin the shell.** Seed dressings like dieldrin killed adults outright.
**A lasting poison multiplies up the chain.** Each animal burns most of its food but keeps the fat-soluble poison, so top predators carry the most.
**Carson's Silent Spring and the bans followed.** DDT was banned in the United States in 1972.
**The peregrines came back.** They now nest on city towers, Seattle's since 1994; other lasting chemicals, like PCBs in Puget Sound's orcas, remain.

collectors.title: Egg collectors
collectors.text: Collecting wild birds' eggs was a common hobby in Britain until it was made illegal for most species in 1954. The collectors' cabinets, carefully labelled, ended up as one of the best records of how birds had changed over a century.

dde.title: How DDE thins a shell
dde.text: A bird lays down the calcium carbonate of its shell in a few hours in the shell gland. DDE interferes with the enzymes and calcium transport there. Birds of prey turned out to be far more sensitive than chickens, which is why tests on poultry had missed the effect.

carson.title: Rachel Carson
carson.text: Carson was a marine biologist with the United States Fish and Wildlife Service and a best-selling author of books about the sea before she turned to pesticides. She had cancer while writing Silent Spring and died in 1964, two years after it came out.

orca.title: PCBs and the orcas
orca.text: PCBs were used in electrical equipment and paints until they were banned in the 1970s. They linger in the mud of industrial harbours. Mother orcas pass much of their load to their first calves in their milk, which is one reason the southern residents of Puget Sound struggle to raise young.
